Here’s how the current process works:
To recall a statewide official, proponents must gather signatures totaling at least 12% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the prior election. For the Newsom recall, that threshold was 1.3 million signatures (https://admin.cdn.sos.ca.gov/elections/ccrov/2025/march/25024ra.pdf). To recall members of the state Assembly and Senate, the minimum number of signatures is 20% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the last election — for Newman’s recall, that threshold was about 63,600 signatures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/administration/news-releases-and-advisories/2018-news-releases-and-advisories/recall-signatures-senate-district-29-certified).
Once a recall qualifies, voters then receive a ballot with two questions — one, should this official be recalled, and two, who should replace them? — and a list of replacement candidates. If a simple majority votes in favor of the recall, the replacement candidate who receives the most votes wins — even if that candidate only gets a fraction of the votes against the recall.
The two-question setup is confusing — only six other states use it (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/recall-of-state-officials). And permitting someone to be elected without majority support is undemocratic. Furthermore, given the distraction and price of recalls — Newsom’s cost about $200 million during (https://apnews.com/article/elections-california-legislature-gavin-newsom-state-legislature-f8b78745cc5376dc4836d914352f2116) the most fraught moments of the pandemic — they should be reserved for cases of serious misconduct or abject unfitness, not petty grievances.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Even though only 11 recalls of state-level officials have qualified for the ballot since 1913, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), California could benefit from raising the bar. Its signature-gathering threshold is among the lowest in the nation (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Reports/266/Report266.pdf).
But Prop 5 doesn’t grapple with this issue.
Instead, it would eliminate the second question from the recall ballot, meaning voters would decide only whether the official should be removed.
If a majority says yes, one of three things would happen:
If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would automatically step into the role. If the recall happens in the first half of a governor’s four-year term before the nomination period ends for the next statewide election, the lieutenant governor would serve until that election takes place and voters choose the next governor. But if the recall happens after that point, the lieutenant governor would finish the rest of the governor’s term.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
If another statewide official — such as the lieutenant governor, attorney general or secretary of state — is recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement. The governor already follows this process for statewide officials who die, resign or accept a different job.
And if a member of the state Legislature is recalled, the governor would call a special election for their replacement — mirroring the existing process for a lawmaker who dies, resigns or takes a different job. As the Legislative Analyst’s office notes (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), if this special election couldn’t be consolidated with an already scheduled election, it could cost state and local election officials “millions of dollars” to administer.
Newman argued to us that eliminating the second question reduces “partisan games” and prevents candidates with minority support from winning elections.
We agree that the second question is problematic and we might support its removal in isolation. But Prop 5 contains a completely unnecessary provision that permits recalled officials to run in the very special election designed to replace them — overturning a ban in the California Constitution (https://law.justia.com/constitution/california/article-ii/section-15/).
This is particularly egregious because incumbents fighting recall attempts can generally raise unlimited funds from donors (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=85315.&lawCode=GOV). Although state law prohibits that money from being used for other campaigns, a recalled official in a special election is unlikely to forget whatever limitless support they received from wealthy special interests.

Newman himself couldn’t explain why Prop 5 contains that provision.
“I’m honestly not sure,” he said. “It wouldn’t pain me if it wasn’t there.”

California’s recall process can certainly be improved, but the problem isn’t so dire that voters need to accept Prop 5’s glaring flaw.

- **Official ballot title:** “Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers.
Legislative Constitutional Amendment.”

Voters answer whether to remove the official and, on the same ballot, choose a replacement from a separate list.
The targeted official cannot be on that replacement list.

### Proposal
As described below, Proposition 5 changes the recall process to make it like the existing process for filling vacant state offices, except for the process to recall the Governor.
***Removes Second Question From Recall Elections.*** Proposition 5 removes the second question—who should replace a recalled official—from a recall election.
This means, in future recall elections, voters would only decide whether to remove an elected official from a state office, not who would replace the official.
***Specifies Steps for Filling Vacant Offices.*** If a state official is recalled, Proposition 5 makes the office of the recalled official vacant.
Except for the office of the Governor, Proposition 5 uses the existing process for filling vacancies to fill the office.
In the case of an office in the state Senate or Assembly, this means that a replacement typically would be elected through a separate special election.
The Governor would choose who would fill a vacancy in any other office (other than office of the Governor).
***Creates Separate Process for Filling the Office of the Governor.*** The process for filling the office of the Governor depends on when the recall occurs.

I need to examine the law text, expert analyses, and editorials before deciding.

Proposition 5 would remove the replacement candidate question from state recall elections. If a governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor becomes governor. If the recall occurs before the next statewide election's nomination period closes during the first two years, voters elect a new governor at that future election. Otherwise, the Lieutenant Governor serves the remainder of the term.

Opponents point out that a recalled officer could run for the same office in a special election. The core issue is California's simultaneous replacement election, where a candidate can win with a plurality rather than a majority.

The 2021 recall provides a concrete example. Larry Elder won about 48% of replacement votes. The 28% figure is misleading because many voters who opposed the recall skipped the replacement question entirely. This reveals a structural flaw in the current system.

The current system allows a simple majority to remove an official while the replacement candidate can win with a plurality. This creates an incentive for partisan recalls to install someone who could not win in a normal election. Crowded ballots and expensive elections further increase the likelihood of plurality wins. The proposed fix has significant drawbacks.

The proposed change would give the governor sole authority to appoint replacements for statewide constitutional officers other than governor. This shifts power from voters to the executive branch. A recall could then be counterproductive if the governor's appointee is more aligned with the governor than the recalled official was.

The Lieutenant Governor is chosen independently of the governor, so they may belong to a different party. Still, they often share the same party. This means a recall could leave the state without an immediate choice for a different direction.

If the recall occurs after the first half of the term, the Lieutenant Governor serves the remainder without a special election. That could mean two years under an unelected official.

Opponents also note that a recalled official can run again in the special election. The SF Chronicle editorial called this particular flaw "so bizarre even its author doesn't like."

The bill would create a separate special election for legislative seats, leaving them vacant and costing millions. Constituents would be unrepresented during that gap.

Josh Newman, the author, was recalled in 2018 over a gas tax vote and later won the seat back in 2020. Opponents see this as sour grapes.

The measure passed the legislature on largely party lines, with Democrats holding supermajorities and Republicans opposing it.

I need to compare this measure against the Little Hoover Commission and other independent recommendations from PPIC, CalMatters, and scholars. Those experts generally favored raising signature thresholds or requiring reasons for recall, and separating replacement elections into later special elections.

PROPOSITION 5
This amendment proposed by Senate Constitutional
Amendment 1 of the 2023–2024 Regular Session
(Resolution Chapter 204, Statutes of 2024) expressly
amends the California Constitution by amending
sections thereof; therefore, existing provisions
proposed to be deleted are printed in strikeout type
and new provisions proposed to be added are printed in
italic type to indicate that they are new.
PROPOSED AMENDMENTS TO
ARTICLES II AND V
First—That Section 15 of Article II thereof is amended
to read:
SEC. 15. (a) An election to determine whether to
recall an officer and, if appropriate, to elect a successor
shall be called by the Governor and held not less than
60 days nor more than 80 days from the date of
certification of sufficient signatures.
(b) A recall election may be conducted within 180 days
from the date of certification of sufficient signatures in
order that the election may be consolidated with the
next regularly scheduled election occurring wholly or
partially within the same jurisdiction in which the recall
election is held, if the number of voters eligible to vote
at that next regularly scheduled election equal at least
50 percent of all the voters eligible to vote at the recall
election.
(c) If the majority vote on the question is to recall, the
officer is removed and, if there is a candidate, the
candidate who receives a plurality is the successor. The
officer may not be a candidate, nor shall there be any
candidacy for an office filled pursuant to subdivision (d)
of Section 16 of Article VI. and the office shall be
vacant. The vacancy shall be filled in accordance with
this Constitution and statute, provided that the officer
who was the subject of the recall election shall not be
appointed to fill the vacancy in that office.

Second—That Section 17 of Article II thereof is
amended to read:
SEC. 17. If recall of the Governor or Secretary of
State is initiated, the recall duties of that office shall be

Governor and Secretary of State are initiated at the

Third—That Section 10 of Article V thereof is amended

SEC. 10. (a) The Lieutenant Governor shall become

(b) Notwithstanding subdivision (c) of Section 15 of

recall, the Lieutenant Governor shall become Governor
for the remainder of the unexpired term. If the Governor

nomination period for the next statewide election during
the first two years of the Governor’s term, a special
election shall be called to replace the Governor and
shall be consolidated with the statewide primary
election and, if necessary, the subsequent statewide

(c) The Lieutenant Governor shall act as Governor

Endorsement: Prop 5 has a flaw so bizarre even its author doesn’t like it
Proposition 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials.
S.F. Chronicle from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 8, 2026
So much has happened in American politics since 2021 that the recall election of California Gov. Gavin Newsom, which he overwhelmingly defeated, feels like a distant memory.
Proposition 5 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot puts recalls back in the spotlight.
Endorsement guide: S.F. Chronicle Endorsements for the 2026 California Election (https://www.sfchronicle.com/projects/2026/california-sf-election-endorsements/)
Also: Y (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/supreme-court-judge-california-22431608.php)es or no? Here are the Chronicle’s endorsements for California Supreme Court and appeals courts (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/supreme-court-judge-california-22431608.php)
Authored by (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1) former Democratic state Sen. Josh Newman of Fullerton — who was recalled in 2018, won reelection in 2020 and lost again in 2024 — Prop 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Here’s how the current process works:
To recall a statewide official, proponents must gather signatures totaling at least 12% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the prior election. For the Newsom recall, that threshold was 1.3 million signatures (https://admin.cdn.sos.ca.gov/elections/ccrov/2025/march/25024ra.pdf). To recall members of the state Assembly and Senate, the minimum number of signatures is 20% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the last election — for Newman’s recall, that threshold was about 63,600 signatures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/administration/news-releases-and-advisories/2018-news-releases-and-advisories/recall-signatures-senate-district-29-certified).
Once a recall qualifies, voters then receive a ballot with two questions — one, should this official be recalled, and two, who should replace them? — and a list of replacement candidates. If a simple majority votes in favor of the recall, the replacement candidate who receives the most votes wins — even if that candidate only gets a fraction of the votes against the recall.
The two-question setup is confusing — only six other states use it (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/recall-of-state-officials). And permitting someone to be elected without majority support is undemocratic. Furthermore, given the distraction and price of recalls — Newsom’s cost about $200 million during (https://apnews.com/article/elections-california-legislature-gavin-newsom-state-legislature-f8b78745cc5376dc4836d914352f2116) the most fraught moments of the pandemic — they should be reserved for cases of serious misconduct or abject unfitness, not petty grievances.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Even though only 11 recalls of state-level officials have qualified for the ballot since 1913, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), California could benefit from raising the bar. Its signature-gathering threshold is among the lowest in the nation (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Reports/266/Report266.pdf).
But Prop 5 doesn’t grapple with this issue.
Instead, it would eliminate the second question from the recall ballot, meaning voters would decide only whether the official should be removed.
If a majority says yes, one of three things would happen:
If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would automatically step into the role. If the recall happens in the first half of a governor’s four-year term before the nomination period ends for the next statewide election, the lieutenant governor would serve until that election takes place and voters choose the next governor. But if the recall happens after that point, the lieutenant governor would finish the rest of the governor’s term.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
If another statewide official — such as the lieutenant governor, attorney general or secretary of state — is recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement. The governor already follows this process for statewide officials who die, resign or accept a different job.
And if a member of the state Legislature is recalled, the governor would call a special election for their replacement — mirroring the existing process for a lawmaker who dies, resigns or takes a different job. As the Legislative Analyst’s office notes (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), if this special election couldn’t be consolidated with an already scheduled election, it could cost state and local election officials “millions of dollars” to administer.
Newman argued to us that eliminating the second question reduces “partisan games” and prevents candidates with minority support from winning elections.
We agree that the second question is problematic and we might support its removal in isolation. But Prop 5 contains a completely unnecessary provision that permits recalled officials to run in the very special election designed to replace them — overturning a ban in the California Constitution (https://law.justia.com/constitution/california/article-ii/section-15/).
This is particularly egregious because incumbents fighting recall attempts can generally raise unlimited funds from donors (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=85315.&lawCode=GOV). Although state law prohibits that money from being used for other campaigns, a recalled official in a special election is unlikely to forget whatever limitless support they received from wealthy special interests.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Newman himself couldn’t explain why Prop 5 contains that provision.
“I’m honestly not sure,” he said. “It wouldn’t pain me if it wasn’t there.”

But it is there. And the inability or unwillingness of lawmakers to put forth a simple, clean reform effort is reason enough for voters to reject this measure.
California’s recall process can certainly be improved, but the problem isn’t so dire that voters need to accept Prop 5’s glaring flaw.

Careful evaluation is needed before deciding.

The current recall system has structural flaws. A replacement candidate can win with less support than the recalled official. Incumbents are barred from running as replacements. The two-question ballot also risks distorting results when voters skip the replacement question.

The signature threshold is too low, encouraging frequent recalls. Gubernatorial recall costs are enormous. Only six states use simultaneous replacement elections. The Little Hoover Commission proposed a snap special recall with all candidates on one ballot instead of the current two-part system. They also recommended raising the signature threshold from 12% to 10%.

Prop 5 does not adopt the Little Hoover Commission's snap special recall. It removes the replacement question entirely. The Lieutenant Governor would succeed the governor, with a special election only if the recall occurs before the next statewide nomination period. For other statewide offices, the governor would make appointments instead of holding a special election. Recalled legislators would still be eligible to run in special elections.

The SF Chronicle editorial board recommends voting no. They find the provision allowing recalled officials to run in special elections to be a bizarre flaw even the author could not explain. Recalled incumbents may raise unlimited funds during recall campaigns. The LA Times commentary appears more sympathetic, so I will read it more carefully.

I will check editorial endorsements from the LA Times, Sacramento Bee, Mercury News, and Orange County Register. I also need to examine Section 15(c) of the constitution more closely to understand exactly how the recalled-officer-ineligibility rule is written.

Prop 5 removes the constitutional ban on recalled officials running for office. It only bars them from being appointed to fill a vacancy. They can still run in special elections for legislators.

Article V Section 10(b) also fails to bar the recalled governor from running in a special election. The Lieutenant Governor would succeed the governor, but the recalled official could still compete for that office.

The deleted constitutional ban on recalled candidates means a recalled governor could run in the special election to reclaim the office. They would retain unlimited fundraising advantages from the recall campaign period.

I need to check how long appointments last for other executive offices. The LAO indicates the governor fills vacancies in offices like the Attorney General and Supreme Court through appointment. I should verify whether those appointees serve until the next election or until the term ends.

Photo by NewsBase via AP Photo In summary Following the failed 2021 recall of Gov. Gavin Newsom, Democrats had the political will and momentum to call for changes to the recall process. What emerged was Proposition 5 on the November ballot, a measure to change the recall process. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Sacramento State political science professor Kim Nalder was working out at a Sacramento gym in 2003 when she overheard a conversation about the upcoming recall election of then-Gov. Gray Davis, a Democrat. She remembers “guys in the weight room just saying, like, “How cool would that be to have Arnold Schwarzenegger as our governor?’” she said. “It had nothing to do with policy at all.” A few months later, the international action film star triumphed in a field of 135 candidates to replace Davis, who’d been re-elected the year before but had come under fire for rolling blackouts in the state and unpopular vehicle license fees. “The Governator” went on to serve nearly two terms. If the election were just about whether or not Davis should keep his job, and not also who should replace him if he were recalled, Nalder doubts the Republican Schwarzenegger would ever have taken office. Accompanying him on the ballot were a host of other colorful characters, including actor Gary Coleman and porn star Mary Carey. Per the rules of the recall, the candidate with the most votes, not necessarily the majority, wins. “I just think the recall probably wouldn’t have happened — because there wasn’t that much upset at Davis himself — if we didn’t, you know, have any fun alternatives,” she said. California voters this year are deciding whether to approve Proposition 5 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-5-recall-reform/), which would do away with “the second question” of who should replace a state elected official if they are recalled. Instead, depending on the office and the timing, a replacement would be appointed or elected in a special election. ELECTION 2026 (https://calmatters.org/tag/election-2026) 2026 Voter Guide (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/) Get ready for California’s midterm election. This voter guide has everything you need to know The measure was placed on the November ballot by Democratic lawmakers in 2024 with the support of the secretary of state and good governance groups Common Cause and League of Women Voters. It came in response to the 2021 attempted recall of Gov. Gavin Newsom. Republican lawmakers voted against it, arguing that it would dilute the power of the voters and add costs associated with follow-up special elections. However, with 14 propositions on the ballot and not a dollar raised so far in support or opposition, both sides may have to rely on voters’ gut reactions. The ‘weak gazelle ’ Aside from the recall of Davis, the only other successful state recall this century was that of the author of Prop. 5, Democrat Josh Newman. In 2017, Newman was a freshman lawmaker representing a purple Southern California district when he joined 26 of his colleagues in approving the gas tax (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article143237054.html), which added a 12 cent surcharge to every gallon of gas purchased in California to fund transportation projects. Republicans fiercely opposed the effort, arguing new taxes weren’t necessary. The bill passed with the bare minimum of votes. Less than two weeks later, then-conservative commentator and now-San Diego Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014) told Orange County talk show hosts that gas tax opponents needed to use the “gazelle strategy,” to begin taking out lawmakers who’d approved the tax. Just the right amount of news Just the right amount of news Get California’s most essential headlines without feeling overwhelmed. Get California’s most essential headlines without feeling overwhelmed. Email address By clicking subscribe, you agree to the terms (https://calmatters.org/about/policies-and-standards/). Sign up for free Δ “We’ve identified that weak gazelle, the slowest gazelle, the one with the limp,” he said. “And that’s Josh Newman, in Orange County.” Why Newman? Because he was elected by the slimmest margin of any senator, fewer than 2,500 votes. In the ensuing weeks, DeMaio’s organization, Reform California, led the effort to recall Newman, helping to collect more than 64,000 signatures — equivalent to 20% of voters in the last election — and centering its campaign on Newman’s “deciding vote” on the tax. Close to 60% of voters chose to recall Newman in June 2018, replacing him with Republican Ling Ling Chang. The recall ended the Democrats’ supermajority in the state Senate. Gov. Gray Davis speaks at an anti-recall labor union rally in San Jose on Oct. 5, 2003. Photo by David McNew, Getty Images In a recent interview with CalMatters, DeMaio stood by his “weak gazelle” strategy. “If voters want to stop something from happening and being repeated, then mid-term, sometimes the only thing they can do is to use a recall as a way of expressing their opposition,” he said. But Newman said that kind of “political gamesmanship” was not what former progressive governor Hiram Johnson intended when he proposed the law in 1911. In a speech (https://governors.library.ca.gov/addresses/23-hjohnson01.html#:~:text=the%20precautionary%20measure%20by%20which%20a%20recalcitrant%20official%20can%20be%20removed%20is%20designated%20the%20%E2%80%9CRecall.%E2%80%9D), Johnson characterized the recall process as “the precautionary measure by which a recalcitrant official can be removed.” Newman said he doesn’t feel he fit that bill. “I didn’t do anything other than cast a tough vote,” he said. “Was I malfeasant? I hardly think so. Especially given the state of the state’s road systems at the time.” Newman made recall reform one of his priorities when he was elected back into office in 2020. After an expensive recall election (https://calmatters.org/gavin-newsom-recall-election/) for Newsom, other Democrats had the political will and Newman put forward Senate Constitutional Amendment 1, which became Prop. 5. Newman said the title of the proposition, which says that it “Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers,” may confuse voters, since legislators do not hold statewide office, though all California legislative races would be affected by the change. How would it work? If Prop. 5 passes, eliminating the replacement question, the governor would call a special election within about four months to replace a recalled state senator or assemblymember. If the governor was recalled within the first two years of their term, the secretary of state would call a special election. If they are in the second two years of their term, the lieutenant governor would finish the governor’s term. The ousted official would be allowed to run for the same office in the special election. If a statewide official such as the state treasurer, attorney general, or insurance commissioner were recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement to serve until the next scheduled election. If Prop. 5 were to pass, DeMaio said the gap in representation may dissuade voters from approving a recall, even if they want a change. “The argument will now be made, if Prop. 5 passes, that if you vote yes on recall, then you’re going to be without a representative for months, if not longer, and so you’re going to silence your community,” he said. He said extra special elections would lead to higher costs to taxpayers. The 2021 attempted recall of Newsom cost about $200 million to administer — a cost that would double if there were two separate elections. However, Nalder suspects the change would lead to fewer recalls in general, likely a guiding force in Democrats’ support of the effort. “It’s relatively easy to get the signatures, and it causes a lot of chaos and costs a lot of extra money,” she said. “That’s easier for Democrats to want to change because they’re the ones who win more in the races.” A Public Policy Institute of California poll in early September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/#:~:text=Proposition%205%20(Changes%20Recall%20Election%20Process%20for%20Statewide%20Officers).) found the measure faces long odds, though: 59% of likely voters said they likely would vote “no” and just 35% said they would vote “yes.” Nalder said the poll was conducted before voters had done their ballot homework, and upon learning more, they’ll likely align with their party’s positions. For the record: This story was corrected to reflect that Josh Newman was one of 27 state senators who approved the gas tax in 2017. That was the tab in 2021, when California held a recall election (https://www.latimes.com/topic/newsom-recall) less than a year before Gov. Gavin Newsom was set to face voters.
There was angst —the COVID-19 pandemic was raging (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-08-19/l-a-county-covid-19-deaths-top-25000-as-delta-spreads). There was anger — the lifesaving restrictions (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-12-13/california-orders-statewide-mask-order-starting-wednesday) imposed by Washington and Sacramento made daily living a chore (https://www.latimes.com/science/coronavirus-one-year-later) and drove many small businesses to the brink. Others went clear over the edge (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2020-10-29/coronavirus-pandemic-small-business-southern-california).
There was also no small amount of political opportunism at play.
The recall gave Newsom’s critics, mainly on the right, a chance to try to chase the Democrat from an office (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2021-08-27/recall-backers-have-california-ideas-beyond-newsom-defeat) that Republicans, under normal circumstances, stood little chance of winning.
Advertisement
In the end, the recall effort amounted to scarcely more than a partisan tantrum. The result — 61.9% voting no, 38.1% voting yes (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-09-14/recall-election-california-newsom-results) — matched the outcome of the 2018 gubernatorial race (https://www.latimes.com/politics/la-pol-ca-california-governor-race-20181106-story.html) down to the decimal. All that money and effort wasted on an election in which voters said pretty much, yep, we meant what we said. Not too long after, they gave Newsom a second term (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2022-11-08/2022-california-election-governor-newsom-dahle-results).
The plebiscite, and its pointlessness (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2021-09-15/newsom-california-recall-election-costly-lessons), underscored the many flaws inherent in California’s recall system. In November, voters will get a chance to remedy at least one of them, eliminating the chance a candidate could take office with just marginal support from voters.

One choice, not two
Currently, a recall election is conducted in two parts. Voters are asked whether a lawmaker should be removed and, if so, who their replacement should be. If the incumbent is ousted, whoever gets the most votes takes their place, even if they fall well shy of attaining majority support. (Which is not out of the question in a large multi-candidate field; in 2003, 135 people were on the ballot (https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2003-aug-27-me-recallqa27-story.html), vying to replace Gov. Gray Davis (https://www.latimes.com/la-100703recall_lat-story.html).)
Among its provisions, Proposition 5 would amend the state Constitution so that voters would be asked a simple yes-or-no question: Do you wish to recall the incumbent? If so, the lieutenant governor would serve as governor for the rest of the ousted executive’s term — unless the recall occurred during the first two years a governor was in office and before the filing deadline for the next statewide election.
In that case, a special election would be held on the same date as the next primary and a candidate receiving a majority of votes would serve out the governor’s term. If no candidate received a majority, the top-two finishers would face each other in a November runoff, with the winner taking over as governor.
Still there?
Proposition 5 has two benefits. It would save taxpayer dollars by consolidating elections and it would enhance the legitimacy and political standing of a replacement governor by ensuring he or she assumed office with at least 50% support.
But there’s still more to be done (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2022-06-23/california-recall-reform-efforts-stall).
Ending political promiscuity
California makes it way too easy to qualify a gubernatorial recall measure.
Of the 19 states that allow their governor to be booted, California is by far the most permissive. Forcing an election requires signatures reflecting just 12% of the ballots cast in the prior gubernatorial contest. In Newsom’s case, proponents needed just under 1.5 million signatures in a state with more than 22 million voters and nearly 40 million residents.
Not exactly a thundering roar.
The threshold should be higher and the reasons for kicking a governor out of office should be more serious, such as corruption, official malfeasance or conviction for a serious crime. Not just because a governor is a member of the opposite party (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2024-03-01/newsom-recall-sore-losers-are-undermining-democracy), orpeople on the losing end (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2021-04-13/newsom-recall-revolt-red-vs-blue-california) of an election are unhappy with the result.

# Proposition 5: Statewide Officers
## Proposition 5: Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
### Summary
The Senate agreed with the changes to the bill sending the proposed constitutional amendment to voters on the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 5.
Proposition 5 would amend California’s constitution by changing the recall process.
Specifically, it would eliminate the part of the ballot that asks voters to choose a replacement for the official being recalled.
If an official is recalled, the office would instead be treated as vacant and filled under the existing state constitution and state law.
Legislative vacancies would generally be filled through a separate special election, while most other statewide offices would be filled by appointment by the Governor.
If the Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor would take over, either temporarily until the next statewide election or for the remainder of the term, depending on when the recall occurs.
### F iscal Impact
Costs could increase by millions of dollars when a recall creates a vacancy that requires a separate special election, particularly for legislative offices.
At the same time, eliminating replacement candidates from recall ballots could save millions in some elections by reducing ballot and election-material costs.

If a state recall of a member of the Legislature was successful, that office would remain vacant until a special election was held.
If a constitutional officer were recalled, the vacancies would be filled by the governor.
Should a future governor be recalled in the first two years of office, the Lt. Gov.
would fill the vacancy until a special election was held.
If a governor were recalled later in the term, the Lt. Gov.
would fill the vacancy until the next scheduled election.
This would be a longer process, but also one that's more thoughtful, deliberate and — most importantly — respects the democratic norm of majority rule.

Sacramento State political science professor Kim Nalder was working out at a Sacramento gym in 2003 when she overheard a conversation about the upcoming recall election of then-Gov. Gray Davis, a Democrat. She remembers “guys in the weight room just saying, like, “How cool would that be to have Arnold Schwarzenegger as our governor?’” she said. “It had nothing to do with policy at all.” A few months later, the international action film star triumphed in a field of 135 candidates to replace Davis, who’d been re-elected the year before but had come under fire for rolling blackouts in the state and unpopular vehicle license fees. “The Governator” went on to serve nearly two terms. If the election were just about whether or not Davis should keep his job, and not also who should replace him if he were recalled, Nalder doubts the Republican Schwarzenegger would ever have taken office. Accompanying him on the ballot were a host of other colorful characters, including actor Gary Coleman and porn star Mary Carey. Per the rules of the recall, the candidate with the most votes, not necessarily the majority, wins. “I just think the recall probably wouldn’t have happened — because there wasn’t that much upset at Davis himself — if we didn’t, you know, have any fun alternatives,” she said. California voters this year are deciding whether to approve Proposition 5 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-5-recall-reform/), which would do away with “the second question” of who should replace a state elected official if they are recalled. Instead, depending on the office and the timing, a replacement would be appointed or elected in a special election. This voter guide has everything you need to know The measure was placed on the November ballot by Democratic lawmakers in 2024 with the support of the secretary of state and good governance groups Common Cause and League of Women Voters. It came in response to the 2021 attempted recall of Gov. Gavin Newsom. Republican lawmakers voted against it, arguing that it would dilute the power of the voters and add costs associated with follow-up special elections. However, with 14 propositions on the ballot and not a dollar raised so far in support or opposition, both sides may have to rely on voters’ gut reactions. The ‘weak gazelle ’ Aside from the recall of Davis, the only other successful state recall this century was that of the author of Prop. 5, Democrat Josh Newman. In 2017, Newman was a freshman lawmaker representing a purple Southern California district when he joined 26 of his colleagues in approving the gas tax (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article143237054.html), which added a 12 cent surcharge to every gallon of gas purchased in California to fund transportation projects. Republicans fiercely opposed the effort, arguing new taxes weren’t necessary. The bill passed with the bare minimum of votes. Less than two weeks later, then-conservative commentator and now-San Diego Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014) told Orange County talk show hosts that gas tax opponents needed to use the “gazelle strategy,” to begin taking out lawmakers who’d approved the tax. Because he was elected by the slimmest margin of any senator, fewer than 2,500 votes. In the ensuing weeks, DeMaio’s organization, Reform California, led the effort to recall Newman, helping to collect more than 64,000 signatures — equivalent to 20% of voters in the last election — and centering its campaign on Newman’s “deciding vote” on the tax. Close to 60% of voters chose to recall Newman in June 2018, replacing him with Republican Ling Ling Chang. The recall ended the Democrats’ supermajority in the state Senate. Gov. Gray Davis speaks at an anti-recall labor union rally in San Jose on Oct. 5, 2003. Photo by David McNew, Getty Images In a recent interview with CalMatters, DeMaio stood by his “weak gazelle” strategy. “If voters want to stop something from happening and being repeated, then mid-term, sometimes the only thing they can do is to use a recall as a way of expressing their opposition,” he said. But Newman said that kind of “political gamesmanship” was not what former progressive governor Hiram Johnson intended when he proposed the law in 1911. In a speech (https://governors.library.ca.gov/addresses/23-hjohnson01.html#:~:text=the%20precautionary%20measure%20by%20which%20a%20recalcitrant%20official%20can%20be%20removed%20is%20designated%20the%20%E2%80%9CRecall.%E2%80%9D), Johnson characterized the recall process as “the precautionary measure by which a recalcitrant official can be removed.” Newman said he doesn’t feel he fit that bill. “I didn’t do anything other than cast a tough vote,” he said. “Was I malfeasant? I hardly think so. Especially given the state of the state’s road systems at the time.” Newman made recall reform one of his priorities when he was elected back into office in 2020. After an expensive recall election (https://calmatters.org/gavin-newsom-recall-election/) for Newsom, other Democrats had the political will and Newman put forward Senate Constitutional Amendment 1, which became Prop. 5. Newman said the title of the proposition, which says that it “Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers,” may confuse voters, since legislators do not hold statewide office, though all California legislative races would be affected by the change. How would it work? If Prop. 5 passes, eliminating the replacement question, the governor would call a special election within about four months to replace a recalled state senator or assemblymember. If the governor was recalled within the first two years of their term, the secretary of state would call a special election. If they are in the second two years of their term, the lieutenant governor would finish the governor’s term. The ousted official would be allowed to run for the same office in the special election. If a statewide official such as the state treasurer, attorney general, or insurance commissioner were recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement to serve until the next scheduled election. If Prop. 5 were to pass, DeMaio said the gap in representation may dissuade voters from approving a recall, even if they want a change. “The argument will now be made, if Prop. 5 passes, that if you vote yes on recall, then you’re going to be without a representative for months, if not longer, and so you’re going to silence your community,” he said. He said extra special elections would lead to higher costs to taxpayers. The 2021 attempted recall of Newsom cost about $200 million to administer — a cost that would double if there were two separate elections. However, Nalder suspects the change would lead to fewer recalls in general, likely a guiding force in Democrats’ support of the effort. “It’s relatively easy to get the signatures, and it causes a lot of chaos and costs a lot of extra money,” she said. “That’s easier for Democrats to want to change because they’re the ones who win more in the races.” A Public Policy Institute of California poll in early September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/#:~:text=Proposition%205%20(Changes%20Recall%20Election%20Process%20for%20Statewide%20Officers).) found the measure faces long odds, though: 59% of likely voters said they likely would vote “no” and just 35% said they would vote “yes.” Nalder said the poll was conducted before voters had done their ballot homework, and upon learning more, they’ll likely align with their party’s positions. Photo by David McNew, Getty Images In a recent interview with CalMatters, DeMaio stood by his “weak gazelle” strategy. “If voters want to stop something from happening and being repeated, then mid-term, sometimes the only thing they can do is to use a recall as a way of expressing their opposition,” he said. But Newman said that kind of “political gamesmanship” was not what former progressive governor Hiram Johnson intended when he proposed the law in 1911. In a speech (https://governors.library.ca.gov/addresses/23-hjohnson01.html#:~:text=the%20precautionary%20measure%20by%20which%20a%20recalcitrant%20official%20can%20be%20removed%20is%20designated%20the%20%E2%80%9CRecall.%E2%80%9D), Johnson characterized the recall process as “the precautionary measure by which a recalcitrant official can be removed.” Newman said he doesn’t feel he fit that bill. “I didn’t do anything other than cast a tough vote,” he said. “Was I malfeasant? I hardly think so. Especially given the state of the state’s road systems at the time.” Newman made recall reform one of his priorities when he was elected back into office in 2020. After an expensive recall election (https://calmatters.org/gavin-newsom-recall-election/) for Newsom, other Democrats had the political will and Newman put forward Senate Constitutional Amendment 1, which became Prop. 5. Newman said the title of the proposition, which says that it “Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers,” may confuse voters, since legislators do not hold statewide office, though all California legislative races would be affected by the change. How would it work? If Prop. 5 passes, eliminating the replacement question, the governor would call a special election within about four months to replace a recalled state senator or assemblymember. If the governor was recalled within the first two years of their term, the secretary of state would call a special election. If they are in the second two years of their term, the lieutenant governor would finish the governor’s term. The ousted official would be allowed to run for the same office in the special election. If a statewide official such as the state treasurer, attorney general, or insurance commissioner were recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement to serve until the next scheduled election. If Prop. 5 were to pass, DeMaio said the gap in representation may dissuade voters from approving a recall, even if they want a change. “The argument will now be made, if Prop. 5 passes, that if you vote yes on recall, then you’re going to be without a representative for months, if not longer, and so you’re going to silence your community,” he said. He said extra special elections would lead to higher costs to taxpayers. The 2021 attempted recall of Newsom cost about $200 million to administer — a cost that would double if there were two separate elections. However, Nalder suspects the change would lead to fewer recalls in general, likely a guiding force in Democrats’ support of the effort. “It’s relatively easy to get the signatures, and it causes a lot of chaos and costs a lot of extra money,” she said. “That’s easier for Democrats to want to change because they’re the ones who win more in the races.” A Public Policy Institute of California poll in early September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/#:~:text=Proposition%205%20(Changes%20Recall%20Election%20Process%20for%20Statewide%20Officers).) found the measure faces long odds, though: 59% of likely voters said they likely would vote “no” and just 35% said they would vote “yes.” Nalder said the poll was conducted before voters had done their ballot homework, and upon learning more, they’ll likely align with their party’s positions. There was anger — the lifesaving restrictions (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-12-13/california-orders-statewide-mask-order-starting-wednesday) imposed by Washington and Sacramento made daily living a chore (https://www.latimes.com/science/coronavirus-one-year-later) and drove many small businesses to the brink. Others went clear over the edge (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2020-10-29/coronavirus-pandemic-small-business-southern-california).
There was also no small amount of political opportunism at play.
The recall gave Newsom’s critics, mainly on the right, a chance to try to chase the Democrat from an office (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2021-08-27/recall-backers-have-california-ideas-beyond-newsom-defeat) that Republicans, under normal circumstances, stood little chance of winning.
Advertisement
In the end, the recall effort amounted to scarcely more than a partisan tantrum. The result — 61.9% voting no, 38.1% voting yes (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-09-14/recall-election-california-newsom-results) — matched the outcome of the 2018 gubernatorial race (https://www.latimes.com/politics/la-pol-ca-california-governor-race-20181106-story.html) down to the decimal. All that money and effort wasted on an election in which voters said pretty much, yep, we meant what we said. Not too long after, they gave Newsom a second term (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2022-11-08/2022-california-election-governor-newsom-dahle-results).
The plebiscite, and its pointlessness (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2021-09-15/newsom-california-recall-election-costly-lessons), underscored the many flaws inherent in California’s recall system. In November, voters will get a chance to remedy at least one of them, eliminating the chance a candidate could take office with just marginal support from voters.

One choice, not two
Currently, a recall election is conducted in two parts. Voters are asked whether a lawmaker should be removed and, if so, who their replacement should be. If the incumbent is ousted, whoever gets the most votes takes their place, even if they fall well shy of attaining majority support. (Which is not out of the question in a large multi-candidate field; in 2003, 135 people were on the ballot (https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2003-aug-27-me-recallqa27-story.html), vying to replace Gov. Gray Davis (https://www.latimes.com/la-100703recall_lat-story.html).)
Among its provisions, Proposition 5 would amend the state Constitution so that voters would be asked a simple yes-or-no question: Do you wish to recall the incumbent? If so, the lieutenant governor would serve as governor for the rest of the ousted executive’s term — unless the recall occurred during the first two years a governor was in office and before the filing deadline for the next statewide election.
In that case, a special election would be held on the same date as the next primary and a candidate receiving a majority of votes would serve out the governor’s term. If no candidate received a majority, the top-two finishers would face each other in a November runoff, with the winner taking over as governor.
Still there?
Proposition 5 has two benefits. It would save taxpayer dollars by consolidating elections and it would enhance the legitimacy and political standing of a replacement governor by ensuring he or she assumed office with at least 50% support.
But there’s still more to be done (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2022-06-23/california-recall-reform-efforts-stall).
Ending political promiscuity
California makes it way too easy to qualify a gubernatorial recall measure.
Of the 19 states that allow their governor to be booted, California is by far the most permissive. Forcing an election requires signatures reflecting just 12% of the ballots cast in the prior gubernatorial contest. In Newsom’s case, proponents needed just under 1.5 million signatures in a state with more than 22 million voters and nearly 40 million residents.
Not exactly a thundering roar.
The threshold should be higher and the reasons for kicking a governor out of office should be more serious, such as corruption, official malfeasance or conviction for a serious crime. Not just because a governor is a member of the opposite party (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2024-03-01/newsom-recall-sore-losers-are-undermining-democracy), orpeople on the losing end (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2021-04-13/newsom-recall-revolt-red-vs-blue-california) of an election are unhappy with the result.

The SF Chronicle editorial board recommends voting no. They find the provision allowing recalled officials to run in special elections to be a bizarre flaw even the author could not explain. Recalled incumbents may raise unlimited funds during recall campaigns. The LA Times commentary appears more sympathetic, so I will read it more carefully.

I will check editorial endorsements from the LA Times, Sacramento Bee, Mercury News, and Orange County Register. I also need to examine Section 15(c) of the constitution more closely to understand exactly how the recalled-officer-ineligibility rule is written.

Prop 5 removes the constitutional ban on recalled officials running for office. It only bars them from being appointed to fill a vacancy. They can still run in special elections for legislators.

Article V Section 10(b) also fails to bar the recalled governor from running in a special election. The Lieutenant Governor would succeed the governor, but the recalled official could still compete for that office.

The deleted constitutional ban on recalled candidates means a recalled governor could run in the special election to reclaim the office. They would retain unlimited fundraising advantages from the recall campaign period.

I need to check how long appointments last for other executive offices. The LAO indicates the governor fills vacancies in offices like the Attorney General and Supreme Court through appointment. Here is our endorsement | Opinion
Proposition 5 seeks to fundamentally change how California conducts recall elections for members of the Legislature and constitutional officers elected statewide.
Such elections have been rare in California.
...
Under current law, voters are asked two questions in the same election when a recall effort qualifies for the ballot.
...
If Prop.
5 is approved by state voters in November, the second question will be eliminated.
In future statewide recalls that gather enough signatures to qualify for the ballot, Californians would only vote yes or no on whether an officer should be recalled.
If a state recall of a member of the Legislature was successful, that office would remain vacant until a special election was held.
If a constitutional officer were recalled, the vacancies would be filled by the governor.
Should a future governor be recalled in the first two years of office, the Lt. Gov.
would fill the vacancy until a special election was held.
If a governor were recalled later in the term, the Lt. Gov.
would fill the vacancy until the next scheduled election.
This would be a longer process, but also one that's more thoughtful, deliberate and — most importantly — respects the democratic norm of majority rule.
It's why our combined editorial boards representing The Sacramento Bee, Modesto Bee, Merced Sun-Star, Fresno Bee and San Luis Obispo Tribune endorse Prop.

Sacramento State political science professor Kim Nalder was working out at a Sacramento gym in 2003 when she overheard a conversation about the upcoming recall election of then-Gov. Gray Davis, a Democrat. She remembers “guys in the weight room just saying, like, “How cool would that be to have Arnold Schwarzenegger as our governor?’” she said. “It had nothing to do with policy at all.” A few months later, the international action film star triumphed in a field of 135 candidates to replace Davis, who’d been re-elected the year before but had come under fire for rolling blackouts in the state and unpopular vehicle license fees. “The Governator” went on to serve nearly two terms. If the election were just about whether or not Davis should keep his job, and not also who should replace him if he were recalled, Nalder doubts the Republican Schwarzenegger would ever have taken office. Accompanying him on the ballot were a host of other colorful characters, including actor Gary Coleman and porn star Mary Carey. Per the rules of the recall, the candidate with the most votes, not necessarily the majority, wins. “I just think the recall probably wouldn’t have happened — because there wasn’t that much upset at Davis himself — if we didn’t, you know, have any fun alternatives,” she said. California voters this year are deciding whether to approve Proposition 5 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-5-recall-reform/), which would do away with “the second question” of who should replace a state elected official if they are recalled. Instead, depending on the office and the timing, a replacement would be appointed or elected in a special election. ELECTION 2026 (https://calmatters.org/tag/election-2026) 2026 Voter Guide (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/) Get ready for California’s midterm election. This voter guide has everything you need to know The measure was placed on the November ballot by Democratic lawmakers in 2024 with the support of the secretary of state and good governance groups Common Cause and League of Women Voters. It came in response to the 2021 attempted recall of Gov. Gavin Newsom. Republican lawmakers voted against it, arguing that it would dilute the power of the voters and add costs associated with follow-up special elections. However, with 14 propositions on the ballot and not a dollar raised so far in support or opposition, both sides may have to rely on voters’ gut reactions. The ‘weak gazelle ’ Aside from the recall of Davis, the only other successful state recall this century was that of the author of Prop. 5, Democrat Josh Newman. In 2017, Newman was a freshman lawmaker representing a purple Southern California district when he joined 26 of his colleagues in approving the gas tax (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article143237054.html), which added a 12 cent surcharge to every gallon of gas purchased in California to fund transportation projects. Republicans fiercely opposed the effort, arguing new taxes weren’t necessary. The bill passed with the bare minimum of votes. Less than two weeks later, then-conservative commentator and now-San Diego Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014) told Orange County talk show hosts that gas tax opponents needed to use the “gazelle strategy,” to begin taking out lawmakers who’d approved the tax. Just the right amount of news Just the right amount of news Get California’s most essential headlines without feeling overwhelmed. Get California’s most essential headlines without feeling overwhelmed. Email address By clicking subscribe, you agree to the terms (https://calmatters.org/about/policies-and-standards/). Sign up for free Δ “We’ve identified that weak gazelle, the slowest gazelle, the one with the limp,” he said. “And that’s Josh Newman, in Orange County.” Why Newman? Because he was elected by the slimmest margin of any senator, fewer than 2,500 votes. In the ensuing weeks, DeMaio’s organization, Reform California, led the effort to recall Newman, helping to collect more than 64,000 signatures — equivalent to 20% of voters in the last election — and centering its campaign on Newman’s “deciding vote” on the tax. Close to 60% of voters chose to recall Newman in June 2018, replacing him with Republican Ling Ling Chang. The recall ended the Democrats’ supermajority in the state Senate. Gov. Gray Davis speaks at an anti-recall labor union rally in San Jose on Oct. 5, 2003. Photo by David McNew, Getty Images In a recent interview with CalMatters, DeMaio stood by his “weak gazelle” strategy. “If voters want to stop something from happening and being repeated, then mid-term, sometimes the only thing they can do is to use a recall as a way of expressing their opposition,” he said. But Newman said that kind of “political gamesmanship” was not what former progressive governor Hiram Johnson intended when he proposed the law in 1911. In a speech (https://governors.library.ca.gov/addresses/23-hjohnson01.html#:~:text=the%20precautionary%20measure%20by%20which%20a%20recalcitrant%20official%20can%20be%20removed%20is%20designated%20the%20%E2%80%9CRecall.%E2%80%9D), Johnson characterized the recall process as “the precautionary measure by which a recalcitrant official can be removed.” Newman said he doesn’t feel he fit that bill. “I didn’t do anything other than cast a tough vote,” he said. “Was I malfeasant? I hardly think so. Especially given the state of the state’s road systems at the time.” Newman made recall reform one of his priorities when he was elected back into office in 2020. After an expensive recall election (https://calmatters.org/gavin-newsom-recall-election/) for Newsom, other Democrats had the political will and Newman put forward Senate Constitutional Amendment 1, which became Prop. 5. Newman said the title of the proposition, which says that it “Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers,” may confuse voters, since legislators do not hold statewide office, though all California legislative races would be affected by the change. How would it work? If Prop. 5 passes, eliminating the replacement question, the governor would call a special election within about four months to replace a recalled state senator or assemblymember. If the governor was recalled within the first two years of their term, the secretary of state would call a special election. If they are in the second two years of their term, the lieutenant governor would finish the governor’s term. The ousted official would be allowed to run for the same office in the special election. If a statewide official such as the state treasurer, attorney general, or insurance commissioner were recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement to serve until the next scheduled election. If Prop. 5 were to pass, DeMaio said the gap in representation may dissuade voters from approving a recall, even if they want a change. “The argument will now be made, if Prop. 5 passes, that if you vote yes on recall, then you’re going to be without a representative for months, if not longer, and so you’re going to silence your community,” he said. He said extra special elections would lead to higher costs to taxpayers. The 2021 attempted recall of Newsom cost about $200 million to administer — a cost that would double if there were two separate elections. However, Nalder suspects the change would lead to fewer recalls in general, likely a guiding force in Democrats’ support of the effort. “It’s relatively easy to get the signatures, and it causes a lot of chaos and costs a lot of extra money,” she said. “That’s easier for Democrats to want to change because they’re the ones who win more in the races.” A Public Policy Institute of California poll in early September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/#:~:text=Proposition%205%20(Changes%20Recall%20Election%20Process%20for%20Statewide%20Officers).) found the measure faces long odds, though: 59% of likely voters said they likely would vote “no” and just 35% said they would vote “yes.” Nalder said the poll was conducted before voters had done their ballot homework, and upon learning more, they’ll likely align with their party’s positions. For the record: This story was corrected to reflect that Josh Newman was one of 27 state senators who approved the gas tax in 2017. That was the tab in 2021, when California held a recall election (https://www.latimes.com/topic/newsom-recall) less than a year before Gov. Gavin Newsom was set to face voters.
There was angst —the COVID-19 pandemic was raging (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-08-19/l-a-county-covid-19-deaths-top-25000-as-delta-spreads). There was anger — the lifesaving restrictions (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-12-13/california-orders-statewide-mask-order-starting-wednesday) imposed by Washington and Sacramento made daily living a chore (https://www.latimes.com/science/coronavirus-one-year-later) and drove many small businesses to the brink. Others went clear over the edge (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2020-10-29/coronavirus-pandemic-small-business-southern-california).
There was also no small amount of political opportunism at play.
The recall gave Newsom’s critics, mainly on the right, a chance to try to chase the Democrat from an office (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2021-08-27/recall-backers-have-california-ideas-beyond-newsom-defeat) that Republicans, under normal circumstances, stood little chance of winning.

In the end, the recall effort amounted to scarcely more than a partisan tantrum. The result — 61.9% voting no, 38.1% voting yes (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-09-14/recall-election-california-newsom-results) — matched the outcome of the 2018 gubernatorial race (https://www.latimes.com/politics/la-pol-ca-california-governor-race-20181106-story.html) down to the decimal. All that money and effort wasted on an election in which voters said pretty much, yep, we meant what we said. Not too long after, they gave Newsom a second term (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2022-11-08/2022-california-election-governor-newsom-dahle-results).
The plebiscite, and its pointlessness (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2021-09-15/newsom-california-recall-election-costly-lessons), underscored the many flaws inherent in California’s recall system. In November, voters will get a chance to remedy at least one of them, eliminating the chance a candidate could take office with just marginal support from voters.

One choice, not two
Currently, a recall election is conducted in two parts. Voters are asked whether a lawmaker should be removed and, if so, who their replacement should be. If the incumbent is ousted, whoever gets the most votes takes their place, even if they fall well shy of attaining majority support. (Which is not out of the question in a large multi-candidate field; in 2003, 135 people were on the ballot (https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2003-aug-27-me-recallqa27-story.html), vying to replace Gov. Gray Davis (https://www.latimes.com/la-100703recall_lat-story.html).)
Among its provisions, Proposition 5 would amend the state Constitution so that voters would be asked a simple yes-or-no question: Do you wish to recall the incumbent? If so, the lieutenant governor would serve as governor for the rest of the ousted executive’s term — unless the recall occurred during the first two years a governor was in office and before the filing deadline for the next statewide election.
In that case, a special election would be held on the same date as the next primary and a candidate receiving a majority of votes would serve out the governor’s term. If no candidate received a majority, the top-two finishers would face each other in a November runoff, with the winner taking over as governor.
Still there?
Proposition 5 has two benefits. It would save taxpayer dollars by consolidating elections and it would enhance the legitimacy and political standing of a replacement governor by ensuring he or she assumed office with at least 50% support.
But there’s still more to be done (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2022-06-23/california-recall-reform-efforts-stall).
Ending political promiscuity
California makes it way too easy to qualify a gubernatorial recall measure.
Of the 19 states that allow their governor to be booted, California is by far the most permissive. Forcing an election requires signatures reflecting just 12% of the ballots cast in the prior gubernatorial contest. In Newsom’s case, proponents needed just under 1.5 million signatures in a state with more than 22 million voters and nearly 40 million residents.
Not exactly a thundering roar.
The threshold should be higher and the reasons for kicking a governor out of office should be more serious, such as corruption, official malfeasance or conviction for a serious crime. Not just because a governor is a member of the opposite party (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2024-03-01/newsom-recall-sore-losers-are-undermining-democracy), orpeople on the losing end (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2021-04-13/newsom-recall-revolt-red-vs-blue-california) of an election are unhappy with the result.

# Proposition 5
## Analysis of Measure
### Proposal
As described below, Proposition 5 changes the recall process to make it like the existing process for filling vacant state offices, except for the process to recall the Governor.
***Removes Second Question From Recall Elections.*** Proposition 5 removes the second question—who should replace a recalled official—from a recall election.
This means, in future recall elections, voters would only decide whether to remove an elected official from a state office, not who would replace the official.
***Specifies Steps for Filling Vacant Offices.*** If a state official is recalled, Proposition 5 makes the office of the recalled official vacant.
Except for the office of the Governor, Proposition 5 uses the existing process for filling vacancies to fill the office.
In the case of an office in the state Senate or Assembly, this means that a replacement typically would be elected through a separate special election.
The Governor would choose who would fill a vacancy in any other office (other than office of the Governor).
